text: I’ll model the fluid as a 60 mm-radius, 200 mm-high cylinder plus four horizontal rectangular ducts. I interpret “40 mm above the floor” as the **port centre elevation** (so each 30 mm-high port spans z = 25–55 mm), and “15° off tangent” as a 15° inward radial component of each inlet axis, all with the same swirl sense. Each duct’s exposed centreline length from the cylindrical-wall centreline crossing to its inlet plane will be 50 mm. The outlet is the 40 mm circular opening in the otherwise closed top; no outlet pipe length was specified, so its patch lies in the top plane. I’ll use a coarse castellated/snappy mesh after building and inspecting the watertight, patch-labelled fluid surface. First I’m checking the installed CAD/export API.

The export helper confirms it will tessellate all patches in one pass, which is essential for welded STL seams. Before committing to the full four-duct boolean, I’m checking the CAD constructors needed to preserve the outlet circle as a distinct coplanar face in the top (rather than inventing an unspecified outlet pipe).

I’ll now build the coarse CAD fluid volume in metres. The duct prisms extend beyond the wall-crossing plane into the chamber only as a boolean construction aid; the cylinder union removes those buried portions, leaving the requested 50 mm external duct length. I’ll also replace the single top cap with two coplanar CAD faces—a 40 mm outlet disk and the remaining top annulus—so the patches are distinct without adding an outlet pipe.

The first shell-sewing attempt failed because replacing a face by two coplanar faces did not produce a valid OCC shell. I won’t carry that failed construction forward. I’m checking the installed split/imprint operations for a robust coplanar face partition before choosing the fallback of a very short outlet neck.
`Face.split_by_perimeter` is available and should preserve OCC edge topology. I’ll test it on a simple cylinder cap first; this is a focused check before rebuilding the full union.

The cap-splitting test succeeded and preserved a valid solid. I’ll rebuild the full fluid with that method. Because a 20 mm-wide straight duct meeting a curved 120 mm vessel at only 15° from tangent has a naturally curved/clipped wall junction, I retain the exact rectangular inlet plane and nominal 50 mm centreline distance to the local wall crossing; the internal construction overlap is limited to 20 mm so the duct cannot emerge through the vessel elsewhere. Any small clipped terminal remnants belong to that duct’s wall patch.

The measured CAD dimensions match the request and all four axes are 15° from their local tangents. I’ll now render the coarse fluid solid from an oblique angle, with edges visible, to verify the fourfold duct layout, top outlet, and overall connectivity before patch export or meshing.

The preview shows the expected tall cylindrical chamber and four low, tangentially skewed rectangular ducts with no duct crossing the vessel. The outlet boundary is coplanar with the top and therefore not visually raised; it is the measured inner CAD face. Next I’ll map each final face back to its explicitly constructed source surface (inlet end, individual duct walls, cylinder, floor, top annulus, or outlet), and verify one-and-only-one coverage before export.

All 28 final faces are covered exactly once. Each inlet retains the requested 600 mm² rectangular area, and the four duct-wall areas are identical by symmetry. I’ll export the 12 named patch STLs in one welded tessellation pass at 0.5 mm chord tolerance, suitable for the first coarse mesh.

The exported union is closed, consistently wound, and manifold (886 triangles; zero open, flipped, or non-manifold edges). I’ll configure a deliberately coarse snappyHexMesh: a 6 mm Cartesian background grid, one surface refinement level to about 3 mm, no layers, and a fluid-side seed at the chamber centre. This should resolve each 20×30 mm inlet by roughly 7×10 cells while remaining quick enough for inspection.
The coarse meshing dictionaries are ready. I’ll create and check the background grid first, before running surface conformation.

`blockMesh` itself succeeded (32,400 uniform cells), but the follow-on background `checkMesh` could not start because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for geometry checks. I’ll add those standard empty dictionaries; no solver or boundary fields are being configured.
I’ll now regenerate the background grid and run the coarse surface-conforming mesh with overwrite, capturing the mesher’s final quality summary.
This OpenFOAM release requires an explicit `features` entry even when feature snapping is disabled. I’ll add the empty list to `castellatedMeshControls` and leave the geometry/refinement unchanged.
I’ll rerun the coarse mesher from a fresh background grid.

The coarse mesh completed with 35,000 cells and no mesher quality errors. I’ll run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect the boundary table to confirm that all 12 requested patch names survived and none is empty.

The binding check passes: one connected region, 35,000 cells, 12 non-empty named patches, maximum non-orthogonality 60.8°, maximum skewness 3.78, and `Mesh OK`. I’ll now render the actual mesh boundary by patch color—not the CAD STL—to visually verify that the snapped mesh retained the four ducts and the separate outlet/top regions.
The converted mesh contains exactly one boundary dataset for every requested patch. I’ll produce the visual check with translucent chamber walls, colored duct walls/inlets, and a highlighted outlet.

The actual mesh rendering confirms four separate rectangular inlets, four individually patched duct-wall groups, the cylindrical chamber/floor/top, and the central red outlet. The translucent wall also shows that all ducts connect into the same chamber region. No requested geometric property remains unchecked; the only interpretation choices were the port-centre elevation and the zero-length outlet boundary plane stated at the start.

The completion gate found one metadata omission: although snappyHexMesh used `(0, 0, 0.10)` and produced the correct interior mesh, the same point was not recorded in `patches.json`. I’ll re-export the unchanged surfaces with that interior seed recorded so the mesh-side choice is independently validated.
The manifest now records the same interior seed used by snappyHexMesh, with unchanged STL geometry and a closed/manifold welded union.
